newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa does not envisage IMF standby help.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa does not envisage IMF standby help.

text.p: South Africa's finance ministry said on Monday it did not envisage applying for an International Monetary Fund standby facility to help with the balance of payments.

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals, addressing a joint news conference with Finance Minister Trevor Manuel ahead of the annual IMF/World Bank meetings, said he expected the current account to improve in the second half.
South Africa still had reserves to help bridge the current account deficit, plus some 15 billion rand of credit facilities which have not yet been used, Stals said.
"That second line of defence (credit facilities) is still available before we come to the third line of defence which would be the IMF," Stals said.

A number of factors suggested improvement in the current account from now on, including a slowdown in gross domestic expenditure, restrictive monetary policy, the expectation that bank credit extension will decline and the likely effects of the depreciation of the rand.

"We believe that the current account deficit will decline in the second half of this year...so far we have not seen very convincing statistics, but we still believe that the current account deficit will get smaller over the next 12 months," Stals said.
South Africa recorded a deficit of 6.9 billion rand on the current account for the balance of payments for the first half of 1996, after 12.7 billion for the whole of calendar 1995.
Finance Minister Manuel said South Africa had been holding preliminary talks on a possible World Bank loan to help its industries compete more effectively.
"Discussions have started, it's early days yet, on a package that would impact on global competitiveness...a support package that will involve the Department of Trade and Industry," he said.

Manuel, Stals and other officials head off to Bermuda for the September 24/26 Commonwealth finance ministers' meeting before attending the IMF/World Bank talks in Washington from September 28 to October 3.
A roadshow to promote the country's planned Yankee bond issue follows from October 4 to 11.
Manuel said talks within the Commonwealth forum of which South Africa is now a member would be a useful learning experience.
He said he was keen to compare notes with Commonwealth counterparts, including India which is seeking to implement a budget-cutting economic plan similar to that unveiled by Manuel in June.
